title: The triumph of Orthodoxy (843)
hookLine: icons restored; Orthodox Christians still process with them on the first Sunday of Lent

cards: On the first Sunday of Lent, in Orthodox churches, something unusual happens at the end of the service.

People pick up icons, sometimes ones from home, sometimes children carrying small ones, and walk with them in a procession around the church. Some parishes go outside, around the building, into the street.
It looks like a celebration, and it is. This is the Sunday of Orthodoxy. It remembers the day, after the long fight over pictures, when the icons came back into the churches of Constantinople.

teach.b: The image-breaking had come and gone and come again. A church council at Nicaea had already defended icons, but later emperors banned them again.
Then an emperor who opposed icons died, and his widow, the empress Theodora, ruled for their young son. Tradition says she had kept icons in private all along.

She called the bishops together, the ban was lifted, and on the first Sunday of Lent a great procession carried the images back in. That's the triumph of Orthodoxy. But what came back was not worship of wood and paint.
The council at Nicaea had drawn a line: icons are honored, kissed, given candles and incense; worship belongs to God alone.

teach.h: HONOR TO THE IMAGE, WORSHIP TO GOD.
teach.b: It borrowed a thought from Basil the Great: the honor given to an image passes on to the one it shows. Someone who kisses a photograph of a person they love isn't kissing the paper.
Some Orthodox writers call icons windows: not the view itself, but a way of seeing through to it. Windows restored.

teach.h: IN THE FACE OF JESUS CHRIST.
teach.b: Paul's second letter to the Corinthians says it this way in the King James Bible: God "hath shined in our hearts, to give the light of the knowledge of the glory of God in the face of Jesus Christ."
For the defenders of icons, the glory had a face. The word orthodoxy means right belief, and Christians use it in more than one sense.
Here it names a feast the Orthodox Church still keeps, year after year, with the procession. Catholics and Protestants have their own ways with images, which we touched yesterday.

how: On the Sunday of Orthodoxy, the first Sunday of Great Lent, Orthodox Christians carry icons in procession around or outside the church, and the restoration of the icons is proclaimed.

practice: Hold or look at an image that helps you pray or remember what matters, an icon, a cross, a photo of someone you love, and do one small thing to honor it: wipe off the dust, set it where it can be seen, light a candle near it if that's your way.
If you pray, let it be a window and pray through it; if you don't, let the reminder do its work.

wordCard.voice: Orthodoxy, right belief. The feast marking the return of the icons to the churches, still kept by Orthodox Christians on the first Sunday of Lent with a procession of icons.
